# Model and source

* Citation: Snowden TJ, van der Graaf PH, Tindall MJ. Model reduction in
  mathematical pharmacology: integration, reduction and linking of PBPK and
  systems biology models. *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 2018;45(4):537-555.
  [doi:10.1007/s10928-018-9584-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10928-018-9584-y)
  (PMC6061126, open access).
* Electronic Supplementary Material 1 (ESM1, PDF) prints the PBPK equations
  (Eq. 15), the system matrix of the midazolam PBPK model (section 2.1), the
  chemotaxis reactions, equations, parameters and initial conditions
  (Eqs. 20-23, Table 1), and the reduced models (Eqs. 18-19 and 24-33).
  ESM2 (ZIP) holds MATLAB symbolic files for the ERK-activation reduction.

The paper is about **model reduction**: it reduces the linear part of a
whole-body PBPK model by balanced truncation and the nonlinear signalling
network it drives by proper lumping, then links the reduced pieces. Its
demonstrations run published models:

* the perfusion-limited whole-body PBPK framework of Jones and Rowland-Yeo
  (2013; packaged separately as `Jones_2013_perfusionLimited_pbpk`), with the
  physiology of main-text Table 1 and three compound parameter sets in Table 2;
* the 11-species E. coli chemotaxis signalling model of Tindall et al. (2009);
* the 99-species ERK-activation model of Sasagawa et al. (2005).

The compounds are hypothetical. In the authors' words, the examples "do not
relate to specific clinical cases of experimentally tested drugs": a strong
base, a weak base and an acid are given the parameters of pindolol,
midazolam and thiopental, and in the chemotaxis example the compound acts
as the bacterial attractant.

**What is packaged.** One model per compound, each the *unreduced linked
model* of the chemotaxis example (Figure 6, "25D"): a 14-state PBPK model plus
the 11-state chemotaxis network. The PBPK half alone also reproduces Figure 5,
so these three files cover both figures.

| Model | Compound parameter set |
|---|---|
| `Snowden_2018_pindolol_chemotaxis_qsp` | strong base (pindolol, Table 2) |
| `Snowden_2018_midazolam_chemotaxis_qsp` | weak base (midazolam, Table 2) |
| `Snowden_2018_thiopental_chemotaxis_qsp` | acid (thiopental, Table 2) |

**What is not packaged, and why** (details under Errata):

* the reduced models (the 3-state balanced-truncation PBPK of ESM1
  Eqs. 18-19, the 4-state lumped chemotaxis model of ESM1 Eq. 31, and the
  7-state reduced linked model of ESM1 Eqs. 32-33). They are approximations
  of the packaged models, and the printed lumped chemotaxis equations do not
  hold their own steady state;
* the ERK-activation example. The rate constants of the hypothetical EGFR
  antagonist that links the PBPK to the ERK network are not printed, and the
  network itself is BioModels BIOMD0000000049 from Sasagawa et al. (2005).

## The as-run model differs from the printed equations

The authors' calculation is not the 16-compartment model that ESM1 Eq. 15
writes out. Four printed artefacts agree that it had 14 states, with no
testes and no rest-of-body compartment:

* the midazolam system matrix in ESM1 section 2.1 is 14 x 14;
* main-text Table 3 starts its reductions at 13 dimensions;
* Figure 6 labels the unreduced linked model "25D", which is 14 + 11;
* Table 1 prints no blood flow for testes or rest of body, and Table 2
  prints no partition coefficient for them.

The flows of those two tissues are therefore not returned: the lung (and
arterial blood) carries the whole cardiac output, but only 88.5% of it is
routed to tissues. That arterial leak, 44.8 L/h of blood, is the dominant
route of drug loss in the as-run model. The printed matrix also has
essentially no hepatic metabolic clearance. Both features are kept here, so
that the model reproduces the published curves. Neither is physiology, and
**these models are a record of the published simulations, not usable
pharmacokinetic models of pindolol, midazolam or thiopental.**

# Population

There are no subjects. The physiology is a single 70 kg male reference adult
(main-text Table 1). The chemotaxis network describes one E. coli cell, with
species concentrations in umol/L.

# Source trace

| Element | Source location | Value / form |
|---|---|---|
| Body weight, cardiac output | Table 1 rows BW, QC | 70 kg, 390 L/h |
| 13 fractional tissue volumes | Table 1 rows FVad ... FVar | as printed |
| 11 fractional blood flows | Table 1 rows FQad ... FQsp | as printed; hepatic artery = FQh - FQgu - FQsp |
| BP, Ka, 11 Kp per compound | Table 2 | as printed |
| Tissue mass balances | ESM1 Eq. 15a-15p, in amount form | matches the ESM1 section 2.1 matrix |
| Testes, rest of body | absent | ESM1 section 2.1 matrix (14 x 14); Figure 6 "25D" |
| Hepatic clearance `clint` | ESM1 Eq. 15g term; value from ESM1 section 2.1 matrix | 0 (Table 2 CLbl recorded, not used) |
| Renal clearance, oral F | ESM1 Eq. 15f, 15p | not printed; absent |
| Chemotaxis reactions and ODEs | ESM1 Eqs. 20a-20h, 21a-21k | mass action |
| Chemotaxis rate constants, K, h | ESM1 Table 1 | as printed (per s, per M s) |
| Initial conditions | ESM1, below Eq. 21 | zero-ligand steady state |
| Ligand input | ESM1 Eqs. 22-23 | u = 1 - L^h / (K^h + L^h) |
| Linkage L = gut tissue concentration | ESM1 section 4 | mg/L used as umol/L, unconverted |
| Output `Cc` | Figure 5 y-axis | venous blood concentration x BP |
| Output `cheyp_total` | Figure 6 y-axis | CheY-P + CheA.CheY-P + CheY-P.CheZ |

```{r load}
drugs <- c("pindolol", "midazolam", "thiopental")
mods <- lapply(drugs, function(d) {
  rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb(paste0("Snowden_2018_", d, "_chemotaxis_qsp")))
})
names(mods) <- drugs
mods$midazolam$state
```

# Check 1: the printed midazolam system matrix

ESM1 section 2.1 prints the 14 x 14 matrix `A` of the midazolam PBPK model in
amount form. Any mistyped Table 1 or Table 2 value, or a wrong flow route,
changes an entry. The matrix is recovered here from the packaged model as a
numerical Jacobian. Each PBPK state is started at 1 mg, and the forward
difference is Richardson-extrapolated over two step sizes.

```{r jacobian}
pbpk_states <- c(
  "adipose", "bone", "brain", "gut", "heart", "kidney", "liver", "lung",
  "muscle", "skin", "spleen", "venous", "arterial", "depot"
)
jacobian_col <- function(mod, j, dt) {
  inits <- setNames(rep(0, length(pbpk_states)), pbpk_states)
  inits[j] <- 1
  ev <- rxode2::et(c(0, dt, 2 * dt), cmt = "depot")
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, inits = inits, atol = 1e-14, rtol = 1e-13,
                       returnType = "data.frame")
  d1 <- (unlist(s[2, pbpk_states]) - inits) / dt
  d2 <- (unlist(s[3, pbpk_states]) - inits) / (2 * dt)
  2 * d1 - d2
}
A_model <- sapply(pbpk_states, function(j) jacobian_col(mods$midazolam, j, 1e-4))
dimnames(A_model) <- list(pbpk_states, pbpk_states)

# ESM1 section 2.1, transcribed as printed (rows = d/dt of the state,
# columns = contributing state; same order as pbpk_states).
A_printed <- matrix(0, 14, 14, dimnames = list(pbpk_states, pbpk_states))
A_printed["adipose", c("adipose", "arterial")] <- c(-0.29, 10.84)
A_printed["bone", c("bone", "arterial")] <- c(-0.76, 10.84)
A_printed["brain", c("brain", "arterial")] <- c(-3.46, 26.01)
A_printed["gut", c("gut", "arterial", "depot")] <- c(-4.70, 31.75, 6.11)
A_printed["heart", c("heart", "arterial")] <- c(-11.15, 8.67)
A_printed["kidney", c("kidney", "arterial")] <- c(-50.85, 41.19)
A_printed["liver", c("gut", "liver", "spleen", "arterial")] <- c(4.70, -10.96, 13.29, 11.21)
A_printed["lung", c("lung", "venous")] <- c(-116.66, 108.39)
A_printed["muscle", c("muscle", "arterial")] <- c(-0.78, 36.85)
A_printed["skin", c("skin", "arterial")] <- c(-0.51, 10.84)
A_printed["spleen", c("spleen", "arterial")] <- c(-13.29, 3.74)
A_printed["venous", c("adipose", "bone", "brain", "heart", "kidney", "liver", "muscle", "skin", "venous")] <-
  c(0.29, 0.76, 3.46, 11.15, 50.85, 10.95, 0.78, 0.51, -108.39)
A_printed["arterial", c("lung", "arterial")] <- c(116.66, -216.78)
A_printed["depot", "depot"] <- -6.11

cmp_A <- data.frame(
  row = rep(pbpk_states, times = 14),
  col = rep(pbpk_states, each = 14),
  printed = as.vector(A_printed),
  model = as.vector(A_model)
) |>
  # 0.05 is the resolution of the printed two-decimal matrix and sits well
  # above the O(dt^2) residue of the extrapolated difference (< 0.02).
  filter(printed != 0 | abs(model) > 0.05) |>
  mutate(rel_diff_pct = 100 * (model - printed) / printed)
knitr::kable(cmp_A, digits = 3)
```

Every printed entry is reproduced except the oral-absorption pair, which is
discussed under Errata. The printed matrix uses 6.11 1/h, while Table 2 gives
midazolam Ka = 1.13 1/h. No entry appears where the printed matrix has a
zero, so there is no testes, no rest-of-body and no renal or appreciable
hepatic elimination. The largest relative differences (0.8%) fall on the
smallest entries, such as adipose 0.2876 printed as 0.29, which is two-decimal
rounding of the matrix itself. The largest absolute one (gut inflow 31.65
against 31.75) is the three-figure rounding of FQgu = 0.146 in Table 1.

```{r jacobian-check}
non_ka <- cmp_A |> filter(col != "depot")
stopifnot(
  # the model has exactly the printed sparsity pattern
  all(non_ka$printed != 0),
  # every non-absorption coefficient to within the rounding of Tables 1 and 2
  max(abs(non_ka$rel_diff_pct)) < 1.5,
  # the arterial column leaks 11.5% of cardiac output, as printed (-24.84)
  abs(sum(A_model[, "arterial"]) - sum(A_printed[, "arterial"])) < 0.3
)
```

# Simulation

A single 500 mg oral dose of each compound, observed to 30 hours. The
observation grid is finer over the first hour, because thiopental
(Ka = 5.64 1/h) peaks at about 15 minutes.

```{r simulate}
obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 1, by = 0.01), seq(1, 48, by = 0.05))))
run <- function(mod, dose, params = NULL) {
  ev <- rxode2::et(amt = dose, cmt = "depot") |>
    rxode2::et(obs_times, cmt = "depot")
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, params = params, atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10))
}
sims <- bind_rows(lapply(drugs, function(d) run(mods[[d]], 500) |> mutate(drug = d)))
sims$drug <- factor(sims$drug, levels = drugs)
```

# Check 2: mass balance against the closed form

Drug leaves the 14-state model only through the arterial leak (clearance
`q_leak` times the arterial blood concentration), because `clint` is zero and
there is no renal term. So the dose that is no longer in any compartment must
equal `q_leak * AUC(c_arterial)`. This checks the flow routing independently
of every partition coefficient.

```{r mass-balance}
mass <- sims |>
  group_by(drug) |>
  summarise(
    q_leak = 390 * (1 - (0.05 + 0.05 + 0.12 + 0.146 + 0.04 + 0.19 +
      (0.215 - 0.146 - 0.0172) + 0.17 + 0.05 + 0.0172)),
    auc_arterial = sum(diff(time) * (head(c_arterial, -1) + tail(c_arterial, -1)) / 2),
    remaining = last(depot + adipose + bone + brain + gut + heart + kidney +
      liver + lung + muscle + skin + spleen + venous + arterial),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    lost_via_leak = q_leak * auc_arterial,
    balance_pct = 100 * (lost_via_leak + remaining - 500) / 500
  )
knitr::kable(mass, digits = 4)
stopifnot(all(abs(mass$balance_pct) < 0.5))
```

# Check 3: the chemotaxis network starts at its zero-ligand steady state

The printed initial conditions satisfy the four conservation totals of ESM1
Table 1 exactly (AT = 7.9, BT = 0.28, YT = 9.7, ZT = 3.8 umol/L). Without
drug they also hold the network at steady state, so the output stays at
6.808 umol/L. The totals must also be conserved during the drug-driven
excursion.

```{r chemotaxis-ss}
no_drug <- run(mods$midazolam, 0)
totals <- sims |>
  mutate(
    a_total = chea + cheap + cheap_chey + chea_cheyp + chea_chey,
    b_total = cheb + chebp,
    y_total = cheap_chey + chea_cheyp + chea_chey + cheyp_chez + chey + cheyp,
    z_total = cheyp_chez + chez
  ) |>
  summarise(
    across(c(a_total, b_total, y_total, z_total), ~ max(abs(.x - first(.x)))),
    .by = drug
  )
knitr::kable(totals, digits = 8)
stopifnot(
  abs(no_drug$cheyp_total[1] - 6.808) < 0.001,
  max(no_drug$cheyp_total) - min(no_drug$cheyp_total) < 0.01,
  all(as.matrix(totals[, -1]) < 1e-5)
)
```

# Replicate Figure 5: venous drug concentration

Figure 5 plots a "plasma concentration" after 500 mg orally. It is
reproduced by the venous *blood* concentration multiplied by BP, which is the
packaged `Cc`. Dividing by BP, as the physiology would require, misses all
three panels by the factor 1/BP^2 (3.6 for midazolam). The points are read
from the solid "Original System" curves of Figure 5.

```{r fig5, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 5 of Snowden 2018 (solid lines: packaged model; points: values read from the published original-system curves)."}
fig5_ref <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug,        ~time, ~ref,
  "pindolol",    1.0,  1.50,
  "pindolol",    8.0,  0.36,
  "midazolam",   1.0,  0.93,
  "midazolam",   5.0,  0.39,
  "thiopental",  0.3,  5.70,
  "thiopental",  3.0,  0.55
) |> mutate(drug = factor(drug, levels = drugs))
xmax <- c(pindolol = 8, midazolam = 5, thiopental = 3)
ggplot(sims |> filter(time <= xmax[as.character(drug)]), aes(time, Cc)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig5_ref, aes(time, ref), shape = 5, size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~drug, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Cc, Figure 5 'plasma concentration' (mg/L)")
```

```{r fig5-check}
fig5_cmp <- fig5_ref |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(model = approx(sims$time[sims$drug == drug], sims$Cc[sims$drug == drug], time)$y) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(ratio = model / ref)
knitr::kable(fig5_cmp, digits = 3)
stopifnot(all(abs(fig5_cmp$ratio - 1) < 0.12))
```

# Replicate Figure 6: total phosphorylated CheY

The compound reaches the gut tissue, suppresses CheA autophosphorylation
through the receptor term, and total CheY-P falls within minutes from 6.81 to
about 0.1 umol/L. It recovers as the gut concentration falls below
K = 2.6. The points are read from the solid "unreduced linked model" curves
(for pindolol and midazolam, from the reduced-model markers that lie on
them).

```{r fig6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 6 of Snowden 2018 (lines: packaged model after 500 mg orally; points: values read from the published unreduced-model curves)."}
fig6_ref <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug,        ~time, ~ref,
  "pindolol",    3.5,  1.35,
  "pindolol",    9.4,  2.90,
  "pindolol",   15.2,  4.50,
  "pindolol",   22.0,  5.85,
  "midazolam",   4.5,  1.40,
  "midazolam",   9.5,  3.10,
  "midazolam",  14.6,  4.85,
  "midazolam",  21.5,  6.20,
  "thiopental",  1.0,  1.75,
  "thiopental",  2.0,  3.65,
  "thiopental",  3.0,  5.20,
  "thiopental",  4.0,  5.95,
  "thiopental",  6.0,  6.45
) |> mutate(drug = factor(drug, levels = drugs))
xmax6 <- c(pindolol = 30, midazolam = 25, thiopental = 8)
ggplot(sims |> filter(time <= xmax6[as.character(drug)]), aes(time, cheyp_total)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig6_ref, aes(time, ref), shape = 1, size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~drug, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Total CheY-P (umol/L)")
```

```{r fig6-check}
fig6_cmp <- fig6_ref |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(model = approx(sims$time[sims$drug == drug], sims$cheyp_total[sims$drug == drug], time)$y) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(diff = model - ref)
knitr::kable(fig6_cmp, digits = 3)
stopifnot(all(abs(fig6_cmp$diff) < 0.5))
```

# The literal readings of the text do not reproduce the figures

Two statements in the paper disagree with the curves it publishes. The
packaged models follow the curves, and these checks pin that choice. If a
later correction makes the text right, they go red.

**Dose.** The main text gives the attractant dose of Figure 6 as 150 mg.
At 150 mg the gut concentration falls below K much sooner, and CheY-P
recovers hours earlier than published.

**Hepatic clearance.** Table 2 gives a hepatic blood clearance (CLbl,
mL/min/kg). Converted to L/h and applied as the ESM1 Eq. 15g clearance term,
it removes most of the drug, and the Figure 5 terminal concentrations come
out several-fold too low.

```{r contrasts}
mid150 <- run(mods$midazolam, 150)
clbl_lh <- c(pindolol = 4.20, midazolam = 8.70, thiopental = 2.02) * 70 * 60 / 1000
literal_cl <- bind_rows(lapply(drugs, function(d) {
  run(mods[[d]], 500, params = c(clint = clbl_lh[[d]])) |> mutate(drug = d)
}))
contrast <- tibble::tibble(
  check = c(
    "midazolam total CheY-P at 9.5 h, 150 mg (published 3.1)",
    "pindolol Cc at 8 h with CLbl (published 0.36)",
    "midazolam Cc at 5 h with CLbl (published 0.39)",
    "thiopental Cc at 3 h with CLbl (published 0.55)"
  ),
  value = c(
    approx(mid150$time, mid150$cheyp_total, 9.5)$y,
    with(subset(literal_cl, drug == "pindolol"), approx(time, Cc, 8)$y),
    with(subset(literal_cl, drug == "midazolam"), approx(time, Cc, 5)$y),
    with(subset(literal_cl, drug == "thiopental"), approx(time, Cc, 3)$y)
  )
)
knitr::kable(contrast, digits = 3)
stopifnot(
  contrast$value[1] > 3.1 + 1.5,
  all(contrast$value[2:4] / c(0.36, 0.39, 0.55) < 0.6)
)
```

# PKNCA

The paper reports no NCA, so the table below is descriptive. It records the
exposure of the as-run model for the 500 mg oral dose of Figure 5, computed
on `Cc` (the Figure 5 quantity).

```{r pknca}
conc_data <- sims |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  mutate(id = as.integer(drug), treatment = as.character(drug)) |>
  select(id, treatment, time, Cc)
dose_data <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:3, treatment = drugs, time = 0, amt = 500
)
o_conc <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_data, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
o_dose <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_data, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
o_data <- PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  o_conc, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 48, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
)
res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(o_data)
nca_wide <- as.data.frame(res) |>
  select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)
nca_wide |>
  rename(Compound = treatment, `Cmax (mg/L)` = cmax, `Tmax (h)` = tmax, `AUC0-48 (mg*h/L)` = auclast) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
stopifnot(
  nrow(nca_wide) == 3,
  # Tmax follows Ka: thiopental (5.64/h) earliest, then pindolol and midazolam at about 1 h
  nca_wide$tmax[nca_wide$treatment == "thiopental"] < 0.4,
  all(abs(nca_wide$tmax[nca_wide$treatment != "thiopental"] - 1) < 0.15)
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Structure follows the as-run calculation, not ESM1 Eq. 15.** The testes
  and rest-of-body compartments are omitted, as in the printed midazolam
  system matrix, the 13-dimension start of Table 3, and the "25D" label of
  Figure 6. Their blood flows are not returned to venous blood. The result
  is an 11.5% arterial leak, and that leak dominates elimination.
* **Hepatic clearance is zero.** The ESM1 Eq. 15g clearance term is kept as
  the parameter `clint`, fixed to 0. The printed matrix shows no more than
  rounding between the liver diagonal (-10.96) and the liver-to-vein entry
  (10.95), and Figures 5 and 6 are reproduced with zero and not with Table 2's
  CLbl. CLbl is recorded in the model metadata, and supplying a value for
  `clint` (L/h) switches metabolism on.
* **Absorption uses Table 2 Ka, not the printed matrix.** For midazolam the
  matrix has 6.11 1/h against 1.13 1/h in Table 2. Table 2's value reproduces
  the timing of Figure 5 (peak near 1 h). The matrix value would put the
  venous peak at about 0.4 h.
* **Unprinted constants are omitted, not guessed.** These are the renal
  clearance and oral fraction F of Eq. 15 and the testes and rest-of-body
  flows and partition coefficients. The printed matrix has zero renal
  clearance, and F enters Eq. 15p only as a multiplier of Ka.
* **`Cc` is the Figure 5 quantity**: venous blood concentration times BP. It
  is not a physiological plasma concentration, which would be divided by BP.
  The venous blood concentration is available as `c_blood`.
* **Linkage units are as the authors ran them.** The gut tissue
  concentration in mg/L enters the Hill term as if it were in umol/L (K =
  2.6 umol/L). No molecular weight conversion is applied.
* **Time.** The chemotaxis constants are printed per second; the model runs
  in hours, so rates are multiplied by 3600 (and second-order rates also by
  1e-6 to convert per molar to per umol/L). The network equilibrates in
  seconds and is stiff. The vignette solves with tight tolerances.
* **Dose.** Figures 5 and 6 are both reproduced with 500 mg. The main text's
  150 mg for Figure 6 does not reproduce it (see above).

# Errata

* **Main text, chemotaxis section:** "the E. coli cells were limited to the
  liver and that this represented the effective compartment". ESM1 section 4
  links the *gut* compartment, and only the gut reproduces Figure 6. With
  liver concentration as the ligand, the required ligand-to-model ratio
  varies four-fold between compounds; with gut concentration it is constant.
* **Main text:** Figure 6 dose "150 mg". The figure is reproduced by 500 mg,
  the dose of Figure 5 and Table 3.
* **ESM1 Eq. 15** describes 16 compartments; the as-run model had 14 (see
  above). The concentration-form equations of Eq. 15 also omit the
  volume ratios that the printed (amount-form) matrix contains. For example,
  15a's arterial inflow coefficient is printed as Q/V(adipose), but the matrix
  has Q/V(arterial) = 10.84. The packaged model follows the matrix.
* **ESM1 Eq. 15m:** the testes term divides by V(testes) rather than V(vein),
  and the rest-of-body term by V(rest of body). These are moot in the as-run
  model.
* **ESM1 section 2.1 matrix, oral absorption:** 6.11 1/h, against Table 2
  midazolam Ka = 1.13 1/h (see above).
* **ESM1 Eqs. 21c and 21e** print the ligand-modulated CheA.CheY
  phosphorylation as `k1 u`. ESM1 Eqs. 20c and 22 name it `k10(L)`, and Table 1
  gives k10 = k1 = 3.75 1/s, so the result is identical either way.
* **Reduced models (not packaged).** The 3-state balanced-truncation model
  (ESM1 Eqs. 18-19) is the reduction of the printed matrix, including its
  6.11 1/h absorption rate. Its gut output reproduces the late phase of the
  midazolam curve in Figure 6. Its venous output does not reproduce Figure 5
  (peak about 12.7 mg/L at 0.3 h against 0.93 at 1 h). The printed 4-state
  lumped chemotaxis model (ESM1 Eq. 31, carried into Eq. 32) does not hold
  its own initial state at zero ligand. Equation 31b carries a term
  `2 (...) alpha9 gamma3 x2`, which comes from adding Eqs. 29c and 29f.
  But Eq. 29f prints the CheA + CheY-P association with the wrong sign: Eq.
  21h has `-k-8 x1 x8`, and the conservation substitution of Eq. 28 cannot
  reverse it. With the factor 2 the printed system diverges. With the
  physically correct 0 it settles at a total CheY-P of 11.0 rather than 6.81
  umol/L, so a further discrepancy remains unidentified. The reduced models
  are approximations of the packaged ones in any case.
* **ERK-activation example (not packaged).** The hypothetical EGFR
  antagonist's binding constants are not printed, and the ERK network is
  BioModels BIOMD0000000049 (Sasagawa et al. 2005). ESM2 provides MATLAB
  Symbolic Math files for the reduction only.
* A literature check on 2026-11-25 found no erratum or correction for this
  article.
